pos: n. (the western Scottish county of the Campbells, two of whose earls were executed for the Protestant cause in 1661 and 1685)
etymology: Gaelic Earra-Ghàidheal, the coastland of the Gaels, from earrann, a portion or coast, and Gàidheal, a Gael.
biblical_def: Argyll is the long western county of sea lochs and islands which was the landing place of the Irish Gaels and the seat of the kingdom of Dalriada; Iona lies off its coast. From the later Middle Ages it was the country of the Campbells, and its earls were among the most powerful men in Scotland. Two of them died on the scaffold for the Protestant interest. Archibald Campbell, eighth Earl and Marquess of Argyll, had led the Covenanting party through the civil wars, crowned Charles II at Scone and then made terms with Cromwell; at the Restoration he was tried on charges arising from that compliance and beheaded at Edinburgh in May 1661, dying with great composure. His son Archibald, ninth Earl, refused the Test Act of 1681 except as it was consistent with the Protestant faith, was condemned for it, escaped to Holland, returned in 1685 in a rising coordinated with Monmouth's, was taken and beheaded in June. The Synod of Argyll meanwhile carried the Gaelic Psalter and the Scriptures to the western parishes. The dictionary records the two executions and declines to make martyrs of them without qualification.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a test as a trial or examination; a scaffold as a stage for execution; composure as calmness; to compound as to settle by agreement; and allegiance as the obligation of a subject.
webster_full: TEST, n. Means of trial; a standard; that by which the character or quality of anything is tried; an examination.
SCAFFOLD, n. A temporary gallery or stage raised either for shows or for the execution of a criminal.
COMPOSURE, n. The act of composing; a settled state of mind; calmness; sedateness; tranquillity.
COMPOUND, v.t. To settle by agreement or composition; to discharge a claim by paying a part.
ALLEGIANCE, n. The tie or obligation of a subject to his prince or government; loyalty.
scriptures: Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
corruption_summary: Western Scottish county of the Campbells, where Iona lies off the coast, two of whose earls were beheaded in 1661 and 1685 and whose synod carried the Gaelic Psalter to the western parishes.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the entanglement of a religious cause with a great family's interest, and Argyll is where it is hardest to disentangle. The eighth Earl served the Covenant and also served the Campbell power; he crowned a king he did not trust and then came to terms with the man who had beaten that king, and he was executed for the second rather than the first. The dictionary therefore honours his confession and does not pretend his politics were clean. The warning Scripture gives is against resting a church's cause on any such man: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). A nobleman's protection is a providence to be used and not a foundation to be built on.

The second paragraph gives the ninth Earl his due and states the limit. His offence was a qualification: asked to swear the Test, he swore it so far as it was consistent with the Protestant religion and with itself, and that reservation cost him his head. The dictionary holds that the reservation was right and the rising of 1685 was wrong, for the same reason it holds against Sanquhar and Bothwell. What he had at the end is what the martyrs have: “they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11). The outcomes themselves are God's disposing and not a verdict on the parties, since “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD” (Pro 16:33), and the right word under such a reverse is Micah's: “Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise” (Mic 7:8). The Synod of Argyll's work on the Gaelic Psalter outlasted both earls and both scaffolds.

pos: n. (the northern Scottish province whose earl, the Regent Moray, governed Scotland for the Reformation and was assassinated at Linlithgow in 1570)
etymology: Gaelic Moireabh, probably the sea settlement, from elements meaning sea and settlement; the Latin form is Moravia.
biblical_def: Moray is the northern province along the southern shore of its own firth, fertile and sheltered, with Elgin as its town and the ruined cathedral there that was among the finest in Scotland until it was unroofed for its lead in 1567 and fell. Its earldom belonged in the sixteenth century to James Stewart, natural son of James V and half-brother of Mary Queen of Scots, who became the chief political protector of the Scottish Reformation. He joined the Lords of the Congregation, supported Knox, led the forces that defeated Mary at Langside in 1568 after her deposition, and governed as Regent from then until he was shot from a window in Linlithgow in January 1570 by James Hamilton of Bothwellhaugh, the first recorded assassination of a head of government by a firearm. Knox preached his funeral sermon in St Giles to a weeping congregation, and the Reformation lost its most capable friend. The dictionary records both the regency and the murder, and names the lesson that the Scottish church was slowest to learn.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a regent as one who governs during a sovereign's minority; an assassin as one who kills by surprise; to unroof as to strip off the covering; an arm as power or might; and to prepare as to make ready.
webster_full: REGENT, n. One who governs; one invested with vicarious authority; one who rules in the minority or absence of a sovereign.
ASSASSIN, n. One who kills or attempts to kill by surprise or secret assault; a secret murderer.
UNROOF, v.t. To strip off the roof or covering of a house or other building.
ARM, n. The limb of the human body; figuratively, power, might, strength.
PREPARE, v.t. To fit, adapt or qualify for a particular purpose; to make ready; to provide.
scriptures: Jer 17:5
Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD.
Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
corruption_summary: Northern Scottish province whose earl James Stewart governed as Regent from 1568 for the Reformation and was shot at Linlithgow in January 1570, and whose cathedral at Elgin was unroofed for its lead in 1567.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the leaning of a church on a statesman, and the Scottish Reformation had done it so thoroughly that one bullet at Linlithgow put the whole settlement in danger. Moray was an able, moderate and genuinely Protestant governor, and his death was followed by civil war, two more regents dead within two years, and years of instability in which the kirk's own discipline suffered. Jeremiah states the principle in the strongest terms the Scriptures use of any practical mistake: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD” (Jer 17:5). The curse is not on using a magistrate's help but on making him the arm.

The second paragraph names what should have been resting where instead, and the psalmist draws the contrast in the plainest available terms: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). The duty of preparation remains, and the dictionary is not recommending improvidence; Solomon grants the horse and denies the guarantee, since “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Pro 21:31). There is a second corruption to record in this province and it is a Protestant one: Elgin cathedral was stripped of its lead in 1567 by order of the Privy Council to pay soldiers, and the building fell within thirty years. That was not reform but plunder, and the dictionary names it as such. The rule that covers both the leaning and the stripping is James's: “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6).

pos: n. (the far northern Scottish county, Norse in speech and law for centuries, left with vast parishes and few preachers)
etymology: Old Norse Katanes, the headland of the Cat people, the Pictish tribe of that name, with nes, a promontory.
biblical_def: Caithness is the flat, treeless county at the extreme north-east of the Scottish mainland, divided from Sutherland by the Ord and from Orkney by the Pentland Firth. It was Norse for four centuries, held under the earls of Orkney, and its speech and law were Scandinavian long after it was nominally Scottish; the place names are Norse in the lowland east and Gaelic in the western hills. Its bishopric was at Dornoch and its cathedral burned with Bishop Adam in 1222 by men resisting his demand of tithes in butter. From the Reformation onward the county's difficulty was simple and structural: parishes of enormous extent, a scattered people, livings too poor to attract an educated minister, and patrons who presented whom they pleased. Whole districts went through generations with a reading minister or none, and the evangelical awakening reached the county late, through catechists and lay exhorters rather than through the parish system. The dictionary enters Caithness to state the famine of the Word in its exact biblical sense, and to name where the responsibility lay.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a famine as a general scarcity; a watchman as a sentinel; dumb as mute; a catechist as one who instructs by question; and a patron as one who has the gift of a benefice.
webster_full: FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
WATCHMAN, n. A sentinel; a guard; one set to watch and give notice of danger.
DUMB, a. Mute; silent; not speaking; incapable of speech or unwilling to speak.
CATECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer; one appointed to instruct in the principles of religion.
PATRON, n. One who has the gift and disposition of a church benefice; a protector or supporter.
scriptures: Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
Eze 33:7
So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me.
His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber.
corruption_summary: Far northern Scottish county, Norse in speech and law for centuries, whose enormous parishes and poor livings left whole districts for generations with a reading minister or none.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is ours and it is structural rather than doctrinal, which makes it easier to excuse and no less serious. Caithness had parishes of a size no one man could visit, stipends no educated man would take, and lay patrons who presented relatives and favourites; the result was a county nominally Protestant and practically untaught. Amos names the condition precisely, and the striking thing is that he names it as a judgment sent rather than an accident suffered: “I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11). Hosea fixes the blame where it belongs, not on the hungry but on those who had the knowledge and withheld it: “because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me” (Hos 4:6).

The second paragraph names the office that was vacant. A minister is a watchman accountable to God for warning the people in front of him, and the commission is personal and unassignable: “I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7). Isaiah's description of what such men become when the office is treated as a living is the harshest in Scripture and the dictionary quotes it against its own side: “His watchmen are blind: they are all ignorant, they are all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber” (Isa 56:10). What eventually reached the far north was the catechist and the lay exhorter, men with a Gaelic Bible and no stipend going round the townships; the dictionary records that the system did not supply them and that God did.

pos: n. (the northern Scottish county whose Strathnaver clearances of 1814 and after drove out its people, with some of its ministers preaching the evictions as providence)
etymology: Old Norse Suþrland, the south land, so named from the viewpoint of the Norse earls of Orkney and Caithness to the north.
biblical_def: Sutherland is the great northern county of mountain and moor west of Caithness, and its name records that the Norsemen reckoned it their southern territory. Its history in the nineteenth century is the most notorious of the Highland clearances. The Sutherland estate, held by the Countess Elizabeth and her husband the Marquess of Stafford, covered most of the county, and between 1807 and 1821 its factors removed something like five thousand people from the inland straths, Strathnaver, Kildonan and Assynt among them, to coastal lots where they were to take up fishing, and turned the interior over to sheep. In 1814, the year the people called the year of the burnings, Patrick Sellar cleared Strathnaver; houses were fired, in some cases over the heads of the sick and aged, and an old woman died after being carried out of a burning cottage. Sellar was tried for culpable homicide in 1816 and acquitted by a jury of proprietors. Donald Macleod, a stonemason of Rossal, published his account as Gloomy Memories. The dictionary records the clearances, and names the part some ministers took in them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to evict as to dispossess by law; a factor as an agent; a strath as a valley; hire as wages; and an inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor.
webster_full: EVICT, v.t. To dispossess by a judicial process; to turn out of lands or tenements by law.
FACTOR, n. An agent employed by merchants or proprietors to manage their affairs and transact business.
STRATH, n. A valley of considerable size, through which a river runs; a term used in Scotland.
HIRE, n. The price, reward or compensation paid for the use of anything, or for personal service.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.
scriptures: And Naboth said to Ahab, The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.
Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
Mic 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
corruption_summary: Northern Scottish county where the Sutherland estate removed some five thousand people from the inland straths between 1807 and 1821, Strathnaver being burned in 1814 and Patrick Sellar acquitted of culpable homicide in 1816.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the clearance itself, and the dictionary names it as theft and in places as manslaughter. The tenants of Strathnaver held their ground by a possession older than the written titles of the family that evicted them, and they were put off it so that sheep might be run at a better rent. Naboth's answer is the answer of every such tenant and Scripture puts it in his mouth with approval: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). Ahab got the vineyard by a legal process with witnesses, and a jury of proprietors acquitting a factor in 1816 is the same transaction; the psalmist has the name for it: “Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?” (Psa 94:20).

The second paragraph names the part the dictionary is most bound to name, because it was the church's. A number of the parish ministers of the Sutherland estate, presented by its patron and dependent on its goodwill, told their people from the pulpit that the removals were the will of God, that resistance was sin, and in some cases read the eviction notices themselves; others were silent. Ezekiel's indictment was written for shepherds in exactly that position: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2). Micah describes the arrangement that produces such preaching, where “The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire” (Mic 3:11), and notes that the men doing it still claimed the LORD was among them. The dictionary records that the people of these straths largely left the established church at the Disruption of 1843, and that they had been given every reason to.

pos: n. (the northern island group, Norse for six centuries, whose cathedral of St Magnus at Kirkwall was built over a murdered earl's relics)
etymology: Old Norse Orkneyjar, the seal islands, from orkn, a seal, and ey, an island; the earlier name was Pictish.
biblical_def: Orkney is the group of some seventy islands north of the Scottish mainland across the Pentland Firth, low, fertile and treeless. It was Norse from the ninth century, ruled by earls under the kings of Norway and transferred to Scotland only in 1468 as security for a dowry. Its cathedral at Kirkwall was begun in 1137 by Earl Rognvald in honour of his uncle Magnus Erlendsson, who had been killed on Egilsay about 1117 in a dispute over the earldom and was almost immediately venerated as a martyr; the relics were translated into the new church and the shrine made Kirkwall a pilgrimage. The bishopric was held from Trondheim until the fifteenth century. After the Reformation the cathedral passed to the burgh of Kirkwall, which still owns it, and the islands were served by the Scottish kirk, though the dialect kept its Norn vocabulary for generations. The dictionary records the cathedral as a building worth keeping and the cult that raised it as a corruption, and marks the islands as a place reached by the Gospel across water from several directions.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cathedral as the see of a bishop; relics as the remains of a saint; to translate as to remove from one place to another; an isle as a tract surrounded by water; and a dowry as the portion given with a wife.
webster_full: CATHEDRAL, n. The see or seat of a bishop; the principal church in a diocese.
RELICS, n. The remains of the body of a saint, or something belonging to him, preserved and venerated.
TRANSLATE, v.t. To remove or convey from one place to another; to remove the body or relics of a saint.
ISLE, n. A tract of land surrounded by water; an island.
DOWRY, n. The money, goods or estate which a woman brings to her husband in marriage; a dower.
scriptures: Sing unto the LORD a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof.
Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
And he said unto them, Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature.
corruption_summary: Northern island group, Norse from the ninth century and Scottish only from 1468, whose cathedral of St Magnus at Kirkwall was begun in 1137 over the relics of an earl killed about 1117 and venerated as a martyr.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the making of a saint out of a dynastic casualty, and Orkney shows the process with unusual clarity because the sources are frank about it. Magnus Erlendsson was killed in a quarrel over an earldom; within a few years miracles were reported, within twenty years his nephew was building a cathedral over him, and the shrine brought pilgrims, offerings and standing to Kirkwall. The dictionary does not deny that Magnus may have been a better man than his rival; it denies that a grave becomes a means of grace, and it names the invocation of the dead and the veneration of their bones as idolatry whatever the merits of the corpse. What a believer is told to look for is not a shrine but a sending, and the islands were in fact reached by men crossing water: “Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature” (Mar 16:15).

The second paragraph is the islands' own promise, and it is one of the few places where Scripture speaks directly to a people like this. Isaiah twice sends the praise of God out to the sea and the islands, bidding men sing “his praise from the end of the earth, ye that go down to the sea, and all that is therein; the isles, and the inhabitants thereof” (Isa 42:10), and the psalmist includes them in the LORD's reign without qualification: “let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1). The method by which such places are reached is seldom a plan; it is usually a dispersal, since “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4), and Orkney received Christianity from Norse converts, Scottish bishops and Pictish survivals all at once. The dictionary notes that the burgh of Kirkwall has owned its cathedral since the Reformation, and that a town keeping a great church in repair for its own worship is the best end such a building can come to.

pos: n. (the northernmost island group of Britain, where the Norn tongue died out without the Scriptures ever being put into it)
etymology: Old Norse Hjaltland, probably the hilt land from the shape of the group; the Scots form became Zetland and then Shetland.
biblical_def: Shetland is the archipelago a hundred miles north of the Scottish mainland, more than a hundred islands of which some fifteen are inhabited, closer to Bergen than to Edinburgh. It was Norse from the ninth century and pledged to Scotland with Orkney in 1468. Its people spoke Norn, a Scandinavian tongue descended from Old Norse, and the islands kept their Norse law until the seventeenth century. Norn died out in the course of the eighteenth century, displaced by Scots; it was never written down as a literary language, no Bible, catechism or psalter was ever made in it, and when it went it left only a vocabulary of weather, boats and fish embedded in the local Scots. Meanwhile the islands were served from a distance, with scattered parishes, a landlord system of fishing tenure that bound tenants to sell to the proprietor, and no resident presbytery of their own for long periods. The dictionary enters Shetland for the same reason it enters Cornwall: a people whose language died without ever having received the Word in it, and the loss is laid where it belongs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dialect as the form of a language peculiar to a province; a version as a translation; vernacular as native; unintelligible as not to be understood; and a dearth as scarcity.
webster_full: DIALECT, n. The form or idiom of a language peculiar to a province, or to a kingdom or state; language.
VERSION, n. A translation; the act of rendering into another language; as the common version of the Scriptures.
VERNACULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as a man's vernacular tongue.
UNINTELLIGIBLE, a. That cannot be understood; not capable of being comprehended.
DEARTH, n. Scarcity; want; need; famine; a general want of provisions.
scriptures: Act 2:8
And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
Amo 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
corruption_summary: Northernmost British island group, Norse from the ninth century and pledged to Scotland in 1468, whose Norn tongue died out in the eighteenth century without any Bible, catechism or psalter ever having been made in it.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption named here is a failure rather than an error, and it is the same failure the dictionary records at Cornwall and Brittany: a church that held a people for eight centuries and never put the Scriptures into their speech. Norn was a real language with a grammar, a poetry and a body of law, spoken by the whole population of these islands, and it went out of use without one printed page of Scripture in it. Pentecost establishes the standard against which that is measured, for the wonder of the day was that men heard “how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born” (Act 2:8). Paul's rule about public worship is equally plain, that “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken” (1Co 14:9).

The second paragraph names where the responsibility lies, because the islands' remoteness is an explanation and not a defence. Welsh got its Bible in 1588 because men decided it should and parliament made it law; Gaelic got its New Testament in 1767 and its whole Bible in 1801 because the Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge was pressed into it; Norn got nothing, and the difference was not geography but attention. Paul's chain makes the omission a matter of sending rather than of hearing: “how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14). What follows where no one is sent is the judgment Amos names, a want that is not of bread “but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amo 8:11). The dictionary records that Shetland was eventually well served, and that by then the language in which it should first have been served was gone.

pos: n. (the Hebridean island whose evangelical awakening from the seventeen-eighties produced the lay leaders called the Men)
etymology: Gaelic An t-Eilean Sgitheanach, perhaps the winged isle from sgiath, a wing, describing its peninsulas; the Norse called it Skíð.
biblical_def: Skye is the largest of the Inner Hebrides, a much-indented island of the Cuillin mountains and long sea lochs off the west coast of Inverness-shire. Its religious history is one of the clearest Highland cases of an awakening carried by laymen. Until the later eighteenth century the island was very poorly served; the parishes were vast, the ministers often non-resident or non-preaching, and the people had little but a tradition of Gaelic piety. From the seventeen-eighties a change came through catechists supported by the Society in Scotland for Propagating Christian Knowledge, through the Gaelic New Testament of 1767 and Bible of 1801, and through the itinerant preaching of men like the Haldanes' agents and later the ministers of the evangelical party. Out of it grew the distinctive Highland institution of the Men, Na Daoine, laymen of recognised spiritual judgment who spoke at the Friday fellowship meeting of the communion season, were consulted on cases of conscience, and in many parishes carried the religion of the people while the pulpit was cold. At the Disruption of 1843 Skye went almost wholly to the Free Church. The dictionary records the awakening and the office together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechist as one who instructs by question; a fellowship meeting as an assembly for mutual edification; to revive as to recover new life; thirsty as wanting drink; and refreshing as the act of reviving.
webster_full: CATECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer; one appointed to instruct in the principles of religion.
FELLOWSHIP, n. Companionship; society; mutual association on equal and friendly terms; communion.
REVIVE, v.t. To return to life; to recover new life or vigour; to be reanimated after apparent death.
THIRSTY, a. Feeling thirst; suffering for want of drink; dry; parched; wanting rain.
REFRESHING, n. The act of refreshing; relief after fatigue or suffering; new vigour or animation.
scriptures: Psa 85:6
Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?
Hab 3:2
O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid: O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy.
Isa 44:3
For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring:
Act 3:19
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
corruption_summary: Largest of the Inner Hebrides, very poorly served until the seventeen-eighties, whose awakening came through catechists and the Gaelic Scriptures and produced the lay office of the Men.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that where a pulpit fails, God raises up the laity, and that He does this often enough for it to be counted a method rather than an emergency. Skye had the forms of a Protestant establishment for two centuries with very little preaching in them; what changed the island was a Gaelic New Testament in 1767, a whole Bible in 1801, catechists paid by a society rather than a presbytery, and a body of unordained men whose judgment the people trusted. Nothing in that was planned by the church that held the parishes. The prayer that fits it is a prayer for a gift and not a programme: “Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?” (Psa 85:6).

The second thing to recover is the kind of people to whom such a blessing is promised, which is not the well-provided. Isaiah's promise is addressed to the dry: “I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed” (Isa 44:3). Habakkuk prays for the work to be revived in the middle of the years with mercy remembered in wrath, asking “O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years” (Hab 3:2), which is the prayer of a man who has seen a long decline and does not expect to be told it was fine all along. The condition remains repentance, for the refreshing comes to those who turn: “Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord” (Act 3:19). The dictionary records that the Men were sometimes narrow and sometimes set up a tribunal of experience beside the Word, which is a real danger in the office; and that without them Skye would have had almost nothing.

pos: n. (the Hebridean island off whose western tip lies Iona, from which the northern English were converted)
etymology: Gaelic Muile, of uncertain sense, possibly a headland or a high place; the Norse form was Mýl.
biblical_def: Mull is the large and mountainous Hebridean island lying off the coast of Argyll, with Ben More at its centre and the long low Ross of Mull running south-west; at the tip of the Ross, across a sound a mile wide, lies Iona. Columba came from Ireland to Iona in 563 with twelve companions and founded the monastery from which the Picts of the mainland and afterwards the Northumbrian English were evangelised; Aidan went from Iona to Lindisfarne in 635 at King Oswald's invitation, and from Lindisfarne the northern English were converted. Mull itself held the Maclean lands and the castle of Duart, passed largely to the Campbells, and lost a very great part of its people in the clearances and emigrations of the nineteenth century, falling from about ten thousand to under three thousand. The dictionary enters Mull chiefly to record what went out from its doorstep: a mission across water from a small island to a dark country, which is the pattern Scripture uses whenever it describes the Gospel's arrival anywhere.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending; darkness as absence of light; to turn as to change direction; an inheritance as a possession; and a monastery as a house of religious retirement.
webster_full: MISSION, n. A sending; the act of sending; persons sent; a station of missionaries.
DARKNESS, n. Absence of light; obscurity; a state of ignorance; wickedness.
TURN, v.t. To cause to move in a circle; to change from one direction or state to another; to convert.
INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; a permanent possession.
MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from the world, for persons devoted to religion.
scriptures: Isa 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
Joh 1:5
And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.

To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me.
Psa 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
corruption_summary: Large Hebridean island off Argyll, off whose western tip lies Iona, where Columba founded his monastery in 563 and from which Aidan went to Lindisfarne in 635; it lost two-thirds of its people in the nineteenth century.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that light is brought into a dark country from outside it, and that this is a doctrine about God rather than a compliment to missionaries. Columba crossed from Ireland to a bare island; Aidan crossed from that island to Northumbria; from Northumbria men crossed to Frisia and Germany. At no point did a people generate its own enlightenment. Isaiah states the whole transaction in the passive, as something done to men: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2), and John insists that the darkness contributes nothing to the process, since “the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not” (Joh 1:5).

The second thing to recover is the purpose named in the apostolic commission, because it is more specific than enlightenment in general. Paul was sent “To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins” (Act 26:18); the aim is a transfer of allegiance and a remission of sins, not a civilising influence. And the ground of confidence that such crossings will succeed is a promise made to the Son before any of them were attempted: “Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession” (Psa 2:8). The dictionary adds the sober half of Mull's record: the island from whose doorstep the north of England was converted lost two-thirds of its own population in a single century to clearance and emigration, and the Gospel that went out from Iona is not a charm that keeps a place prosperous.

pos: n. (the Perthshire highland district whose men formed the bulk of the Highland Host quartered on the covenanting west in 1678)
etymology: Gaelic Ath Fhòdla, new Ireland, from ath, again or second, and Fòdla, a poetic name for Ireland.
biblical_def: Atholl is the great highland district of northern Perthshire, running from Dunkeld up Strathtay and over the passes to Badenoch, and its name means new Ireland. Its earls and afterwards its dukes, the Murrays, could raise a large force of tenants from the straths. In January 1678 the Scottish Privy Council, unable to suppress the field meetings of the south-west by regular troops, resolved on a different method: some six to eight thousand Highlanders, the greater part of them Atholl men under the Marquess of Atholl, were marched into Ayrshire, Renfrewshire and Lanarkshire and quartered free upon the people, with orders to disarm them and to compel bonds of peace. They took what they wanted for six weeks, stripped houses, drove cattle and went home loaded; the episode is remembered as the Highland Host. In 1689 a government garrison under Cleland beat the Jacobites at Dunkeld in the same district. The dictionary records the Host as a persecution carried out by one part of a nation upon another, and names it as such.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to quarter as to lodge soldiers; free quarter as lodging without payment; a bond as a written obligation; spoil as plunder; and to oppress as to burden with unreasonable impositions.
webster_full: QUARTER, v.t. To lodge; to fix on a temporary dwelling; to station soldiers for lodging.
FREE QUARTER, n. Lodging and provisions taken by soldiers without payment to the inhabitants.
BOND, n. An obligation imposing a moral duty; a writing under seal by which a person binds himself.
SPOIL, n. That which is taken from others by violence; plunder; pillage; booty.
OPPRESS, v.t. To load or burden with unreasonable impositions; to treat with unjust severity or hardship.
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Jam 1:20
For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.
corruption_summary: Perthshire highland district whose men made up the bulk of the six to eight thousand Highlanders quartered free on Ayrshire, Renfrewshire and Lanarkshire for six weeks in 1678 to break the field meetings.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the use of an irregular force to do what the law could not, and the dictionary names it as plunder authorised by a council. The Highland Host was not a campaign against an enemy; it was the billeting of armed men on the households of their own countrymen, with licence to take their keep and orders to extract bonds, for the purpose of frightening a district out of attending sermons. Scripture allows the magistrate a sword for a stated end, and the statement is restrictive: “he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). Free quarter upon the innocent to deter the lawful is not that. What it produces in a people is the thing Solomon treats as the index of bad government: “when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).

The second paragraph names the fault on the side of the men who marched, because the dictionary does not let tenants hide behind their chiefs. The Atholl men went because their landlords called them out and because there was spoil in it, and six weeks of taking what they liked from Presbyterian farms was a transaction they understood perfectly well. James removes the excuse that it was done in a cause: “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20), and the Host was not even wrath, only appetite with a warrant. The requirement laid on everybody involved, councillor, marquess and tenant alike, is stated in one line and leaves nothing over: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The dictionary records that the Host failed in its object, that the field meetings continued and grew, and that eleven years later Highlanders and Lowlanders were shooting at each other in Dunkeld in a different quarrel altogether.

pos: n. (the Perthshire cathedral town to which Columba's relics were brought from Iona about 849, making it the religious centre of the Scots)
etymology: Gaelic Dùn Chailleann, the fort of the Caledonians, from dùn, a fort, and the tribal name.
biblical_def: Dunkeld is the small cathedral town where the Tay comes out of the Highlands into Strathmore, and for a time it was the chief religious place in Scotland. When Norse raiding made Iona untenable, Kenneth mac Alpin is recorded as having brought a part of Columba's relics to Dunkeld about 849 and built a church for them; the abbot of Dunkeld became one of the great men of the kingdom, and the primacy afterwards passed to St Andrews. The cathedral, built between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, was gutted in 1560 when the Lords of the Congregation ordered the removal of its images and altars, and only the choir was later roofed again for the parish. In August 1689 a newly raised Cameronian regiment under William Cleland held the town against a far larger Jacobite force in a day of street fighting; Cleland was killed and the Jacobite advance was stopped. The dictionary records the removal of the relics from Iona as the plainest demonstration that a religion attached to objects must keep moving them, and names that as the opposite of the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a relic as the remains of a saint; a shrine as a case for sacred things; to venerate as to regard with reverential respect; an image as a representation; and an idol as an object of worship besides God.
webster_full: RELIC, n. That which remains; the body of a deceased person, or some part of it, preserved with veneration.
SHRINE, n. A case, box or receptacle for sacred things; the tomb of a saint resorted to by devotees.
VENERATE, v.t. To regard with reverential respect; to reverence; to treat with the highest respect.
IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device.
Jer 10:5
They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good.
Little children, keep yourselves from idols. Amen.
corruption_summary: Perthshire cathedral town to which part of Columba's relics were carried from Iona about 849 when Norse raiding made the island untenable, and whose cathedral was stripped of images in 1560.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the cult of relics, and Dunkeld exhibits its central absurdity better than any English shrine. A religion whose holiness is lodged in bones must evacuate them when the enemy comes. Columba's remains were divided and carried about, part going to Ireland and part up the Tay to a fort in Perthshire, and the primacy of the Scottish church followed the bones rather than any doctrine or office; when the bones moved, the centre moved. The commandment covers the whole class of such objects and forbids both their making and their use: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). John closes his epistle with the shortest possible application: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1Jn 5:21).

The second paragraph gives the reasoning, because the dictionary prefers to argue rather than merely to prohibit. Paul at Athens denies that the divine nature can be represented in material at all, since “we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device” (Act 17:29); if that holds of God it holds of anything made to carry access to Him. Jeremiah adds the mockery and with it a real comfort, that the object is inert in both directions, carried because it cannot walk, and so “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5). The dictionary notes that when the images and altars went out of Dunkeld cathedral in 1560 the choir was roofed for a congregation, and that a hundred and twenty-nine years later a regiment raised out of the covenanting societies died in its streets for a cause that needed no relics at all.
